title: eStep: Elementary Euclidean-Step Matrix
content: eStep q = !![0, 1; 1, -q] is the 2×2 integer matrix encoding one division step of the Euclidean algorithm with quotient q. eStep_det shows its determinant is -1 (via Matrix.det_fin_two_of, 0·(-q) - 1·1). eStep_apply computes its action on a column: eStep q *ᵥ ![a, b] = ![b, a - q·b], proved by expanding the matrix–vector product with dotProduct and Fin.sum_univ_two and closing with ring.

title: eStep_euclid: One Euclidean Round as a Matrix Step
content: Specialising the quotient to q = a / b turns the elementary step into exactly one round of the Euclidean algorithm: eStep (a/b) *ᵥ ![a, b] = ![b, a % b]. The proof rewrites with eStep_apply and then uses Int.emod_def (a % b = a - b·(a/b)) plus ring to identify a - (a/b)·b with a % b. This is the precise sense in which 'the algorithm corresponds to matrices': each step is a matrix multiplication.
mathContext: $\text{eStep}(\lfloor a/b \rfloor)\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} b \\ a \bmod b \end{pmatrix}$

title: det_mul_unimodular: Unimodular Matrices Are Closed Under Multiplication
content: Because the determinant is multiplicative (Matrix.det_mul: det (M·N) = det M · det N), integer matrices of determinant ±1 form a multiplicatively closed set. The proof splits on the four sign combinations of det M and det N and closes each with omega. Consequently the composite of all the elementary steps of a Euclidean run is again unimodular — the algebraic reason the algorithm stays inside SL₂(ℤ) up to sign.

title: bezoutMatrix: The Bézout Coefficient Matrix
content: bezoutMatrix a b = !![gcdA a b, gcdB a b; -b/g, a/g] with g = gcd a b. Its top row is the pair of Bézout coefficients (from Mathlib's Int.gcdA / Int.gcdB, satisfying a·gcdA + b·gcdB = g); its bottom row is (-b/g, a/g), the exact integer divisions that are legitimate because g divides both a and b. This matrix is the accumulated transform of a full Euclidean run.
mathContext: $\text{bezoutMatrix}(a,b) = \begin{pmatrix} x & y \\ -b/g & a/g \end{pmatrix}, \quad g = \gcd(a,b),\ ax + by = g$

title: bezoutMatrix_det: The Bézout Matrix Lies in SL₂(ℤ)
content: det (bezoutMatrix a b) = 1 for (a,b) ≠ (0,0). By Matrix.det_fin_two_of the determinant equals gcdA·(a/g) + gcdB·(b/g). Multiplying through by g and using Int.ediv_mul_cancel to replace (a/g)·g by a and (b/g)·g by b turns this into a·gcdA + b·gcdB = g, which is Bézout's identity (Int.gcd_eq_gcd_ab); cancelling the nonzero g with mul_left_cancel₀ yields determinant exactly 1.

title: bezoutMatrix_mulVec: Reduction of the Input Column
content: bezoutMatrix a b *ᵥ ![a, b] = ![gcd a b, 0]. Using the helper mulVec_two, the first component is gcdA·a + gcdB·b, which equals gcd a b by Bézout's identity (linear_combination). The second component is (-b/g)·a + (a/g)·b; multiplying by g and clearing the exact divisions gives -a·b + b·a = 0, so cancelling the nonzero g shows the component vanishes. This is the algorithm's endpoint: the gcd on top, zero below.
mathContext: $\begin{pmatrix} x & y \\ -b/g & a/g \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} ax + by \\ (-ab + ab)/g \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} g \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$

title: bezout_unimodular_reduction: Matrix Form of Bézout's Identity
content: The capstone. bezoutSL packages the Bézout matrix with its determinant-1 proof as an element of Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ. The main theorem then states: for (a,b) ≠ (0,0) there exists M ∈ SL₂(ℤ) with M *ᵥ ![a, b] = ![gcd a b, 0]. This is the answer to the parent's open question — the extended Euclidean algorithm is a single unimodular transformation, and Bézout's coefficients are the top row of that SL₂(ℤ) matrix.
